To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have shown that Aβ, a protein associated with AD and CAA, can accumulate in the brains and blood vessels of around 50 % of hGH-iatrogenic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (iCJD) patients and that Aβ accumulation in the brain is independent of the prion protein.
we have found Aβ deposition in the brains of patients who received hGH for treatment of growth hormone deficiency, which is consistent with the hypothesis Aβ seeding can cause AD and CAA.

Aβ accumulation in the brains and blood vessels was found in 18/35 (52%) of hGH-iatrogenic Cjd (hGH-iCJD) cases and in 5/11 (45%) of hGH recipients who had died from other causes, but not in age-matched sporadic CJD (sCJD) or variant CJD (vCJD) patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neuropathology of hGH-iatrogenic Cjd.
the transmission of CJD and other neurodegenerative diseases, such as AD.
the transmission of human prion diseases and the neuropathological effects of human growth hormone (hGh) treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Aβ accumulation was a frequent feature in hGH-iCJ patients, and that the presence of Aβ in pituitary glands and hGH preparations could be a factor contributing to its transmission to the brains of hGH recipients, but that the presence of the Aβ protein in the brains of hgh-iCJD patients does not prove that it was transmitted by hGH preparations.
Aβ seeding occurred in the brains of hGH recipients and that it was independent of the presence of prion seeding.
the Aβ accumulation in the brains of hGH-iCID cases was a consequence of the seeding properties of A β and was not the result of the abnormal PrP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the hGH-iCJDiCJDiCJD patients in this cohort had a high frequency (54.5%) of cerebral amyloid angiopathies (CAA) and AD-like changes in the brain and this is consistent with the hypothesis of Aβ seeding.
the hGH recipients in the UK cohort were a unique group of patients who were inoculated with a mixture of abnormal prion protein and amyloid-β protein.
hGH recipients in the UK had a higher prevalence of AD and CCAA than age-matched sporadic CJD patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Aβ protein can seed in the brain and that this seeding can occur in the absence of prion seeding.
Aβ seeding is not restricted to the brains of patients with AD, and that Aβ seeding and accumulation in the brain may be more common than previously thought.
the Aβ protein is capable of seeding independently of the abnormal prions and can lead to the accumulation of Aβ in the human brain.
